title: National Institutes of Health Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Aug. 9, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of an interview with National Institutes of Health Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Aug. 9, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of an interview with National Institutes of Health Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Aug. 9, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We're joined now by the Director of the National Institutes of Health, Dr. Jay Bhattacharya. Good morning to you, doctor.
NIH DIRECTOR DR. JAY BHATTACHARYA: Good morning.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And we should mention you are also helping to run the CDC until the new director is sworn in as well.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: Until next Wednesday, yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Until next Wednesday. So let me ask you about a number of things that I think people at home are worried about, particularly around the food supply. The cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce from Mexico is now in 15 states. There were two deaths this week due to it. Yesterday, USDA issued an alert for a range of products that may have salmonella, including meat and poultry. 27 states are affected by salmonella, possibly linked to jalapeños, but cilantro, red onion, avocado, also listed in the CDC notice. Albertsons, a grocery store, just recalled some items. There's risk of salmonella in eggs in Texas, according to the CDC, and then you have the screwworm outbreak affecting beef. This is overwhelming for someone going into a grocery store right now. Why do they seem out of control?

DR. BHATTACHARYA: Well, the- the cyclospora outbreak is larger than in normal years. I mean, in normal years there actually is a- cyclospora cases. The- the two deaths that you mentioned, they happened in late July- late- late June, early July, before we identified this source. And so, folks that are listening, can rest assured, the CDC and the FDA are working hard to trace back exactly where these outbreaks are occurring from, intervening with the- the sort of suppliers to make sure that they don't- and doing recalls to make sure that the disease doesn't- the, you know, condition doesn't spread. I mean, it's tough. You go to grocery store, you buy lettuce, and you say, "Okay, can I buy the lettuce?"
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

DR. BHATTACHARYA: And what I say to folks listening, we're working hard to make sure that the contaminated sources don't get onto the shelves. And if you're worried, you can buy that- buy the lettuce, but make sure you wash it carefully. You don't eat outer leaves. And if you're really worried, just, you know, cook your vegetables.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But we're not hearing from the FDA. I mean, should there be a restriction on imports from central Mexico right now? It seems like a lot of things are tied back.

DR. BHATTACHARYA: Yeah, I mean, I think the key thing is that when we find a contaminated source, we intervene. I can't speak for the FDA, thank God. It's just the NIH and the CDC. But, but, but I can say that- that the folks who I have worked with at the FDA are- they're great team of folks that are- they're tracking back and finding the source of these outbreaks. And for cyclospora specifically, it's complicated because for technical reasons, it's much- it's more difficult than if it was just a bacteria to find the exact source. But they've done a great job finding it, and they've been cooperating with the CDC team that I've led the last few months to try to identify the source, and you know, it's- what we know now is because--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: --of that hard work that's gone on.

MARGARET BRENNAN: --But there are also a number of other health issues, including measles cases now at their highest level in 35 years. The CDC says only 10 U.S. states have measles vaccine coverage rates above the 95% threshold in the prior school year. That is so key because that is, as you know, a marker for basically a way to stop transmission, herd immunity. Do you believe that the federal government needs to make a really full-throated push to tell parents, 'go get your kids vaccinated with the MMR vaccine?'

DR. BHATTACHARYA: You know, one of the first things I did as CDC director, I think it was back in February of this year, was that there was a big outbreak in South Carolina, and I went on to- went on- I don't know if TV is the right word, but I went on camera and I recommended that the best way to end the measles outbreak there was to have their parents vaccinate their kids for measles.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: And the outbreak has now ended in South Carolina in part because of that. There's been a lot of- a lot of outbreaks, not just the United States, but around the world.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

DR. BHATTACHARYA: And you know, a lot of that has to do with sort of a collapse in sort of public trust in a lot of science, you know, public health measures that occurred during the pandemic for reasons we can- we can discuss. For me the most important thing is to try to regain that trust.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right, but why not- you can have TV ads. You can have something that's more of a national push. It was notable last week that Secretary Kennedy went on television and did say parents should get kids vaccinated for measles because it's effective at preventing infection roughly 97% of the time. That was a change for him. He has not always been that clear, as you know. Why not blast that across the airwaves of America?

DR. BHATTACHARYA: I mean, I think that I've done my best to try to do that. Every time anyone's asked me about vaccinating their kids for measles, I say exactly that. That the best way to protect your kids from measles is to get the vaccine for- for measles. You know--
MARGARET BRENNAN: This country is going to lose its measles elimination status--
DR. BHATTACHARYA: As did Canada, as did Mexico, as did the UK.
MARGARET BRENNAN : But that's not acceptable, right? The gold standard science--
DR. BHATTACHARYA: But you know, I think the thing is,
MARGARET BRENNAN: --that MAHA wants to--

DR. BHATTACHARYA:--if you look at the actual- what's happened, like the- the- there's specific states where you've had these outbreaks. Big, big outbreak in Texas, which has now been addressed. Big outbreak in Arizona and Utah, that's been addressed. South Carolina, that's been addressed. Now, what we saw was an outbreak in Virginia, again coming down sharply, and now Pennsylvania- is specific communities of people that have- that are the highest risk that we have to focus on, as well as the broader sort of message that it's important for children to be vaccinated for the measles if we want to address the measles outbreak.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, that's why I brought up herd immunity because it puts everyone at risk, right?
DR. BHATTACHARYA: Yeah.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Not just people. But on- on this issue, you were down in Atlanta this past week. This is one year since that horrific shooting at CDC headquarters. Officer David Rose was honored this past week. He was killed last year protecting CDC employees from a gunman. And we should note he was a combat veteran, a United States Marine who had just graduated five months prior from the police academy. Three kids left behind. The shooter was motivated by misinformation about the COVID vaccine. That is why he shot over 100 bullets into the windows of the CDC. Is enough being done to counter this kind of misinformation?

DR. BHATTACHARYA: I mean, I should start with- I got to talk with Officer Rose's wife a few months back. The- one of the first things I did is I- you know, to honor him and his sacrifice in protecting the people that work at the CDC, the amazing people who work the CDC was we, you know, renamed the street that leads into the CDC after him, and it was a really nice event. I'll tell you the- the thing is I want to focus on attention on Officer Rose because I don't- I think the shooter did was horrific, and I think the- you know, you can talk about why shooters do things, but really fundamentally--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, his father said he was brainwashed about the COVID vaccine and thought it was making him suicidal. That's what his--
DR. BHATTACHARYA: I mean the thing is, it's like- to talk about the shooter puts the--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --motivation was when he said he was going to shoot up the CDC.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: --emphasis on somebody who's- I mean, I think we shouldn't be putting our emphasis on--
MARGARET BRENNAN: No, I am on misinformation about vaccines.

DR. BHATTACHARYA: I mean, I think the key- the key thing is there's a loss of public trust in public health that happened in part because of a lot of- frankly, even- even- even on this network and on other networks, there was a particular single point of view put across during the COVID pandemic about how, you know, that led to things that really did cause harm to people. The school closures are probably the number one thing that- that- that--
MARGARET BRENNAN: This is not a productive line of claims. We covered COVID in depth on this program, like no other Sunday show did.

DR. BHATTACHARYA: I'm not blaming you specifically. What I'm saying is, you want to talk about misinformation? The- the- the- the kinds of decisions and sort of the public sort of face of public health during the pandemic led to many people losing trust in public health.
MARGARET BRENNAN: The Trump administration officials.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: No, I mean- I mean, like Biden. So Biden, for instance, censored me--
MARGARET BRENNAN: The pandemic began under the Trump administration, and we put those officials on our air.

DR. BHATTACHARYA: But- but during the- during the- just so we're clear, the Biden administration censored me, right? They censored- they sent out direct attacks on people who disagreed on- on- on the COVID- on- on sort of whether the COVID vaccine stopped--
MARGARET BRENNAN: RFK Jr. called the COVID vaccine the deadliest vaccine ever made.
[CROSSTALK]
MARGARET BRENNAN: That is misinformation, and we're not being clear about that. And I think that is dangerous. Wouldn't you agree?
DR. BHATTACHARYA: People lost their jobs, Margaret, because the- the Biden administration censored people and said, "Look, you can't even talk about COVID vaccine harms.--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --We're talking about a shooting.

DR. BHATTACHARYA: Yeah, and I'm talking about why you have the the kind of distrust that's led to the kind of sort of problems that you're talking- we were talking about earlier in public health. That distrust was not caused by President Trump, it wasn't caused by Bobby. It was caused by a lot of- sort of really fundamental--
MARGARET  BRENNAN: Misinformation--

DR. BHATTACHARYA: Yeah, but often spread by the government itself regarding natural immunity, closures of schools, closures- of mask mandates, people lost their jobs because of these vaccine mandates that didn't make any public health sense. So, if you want to talk about public trust, you have to embrace that fully, right? You can't just talk about it in a narrow political way.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm talking about a shooting at the CDC and an officer, you said you just went to honor. That's what I was talking about. You're talking about something else entirely.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: No, no, you're trying to- you're trying to- just to be blunt--
MARGARET BRENNAN: I also asked you about the shoring up public [inaud]--
DR. BHATTACHARYA: --What you're talking about is you're trying to blame the shooting on Bobby.
MARGARET BRENNAN: No, I'm not. I'm reading you what his father said.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: No, what you're reading, what you're- what you're saying- what you're implying is that somehow the lack of public trust
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm not talking about him. I'm talking about your visit.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: Yeah.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And is enough being done.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: I think it's really unfortunate--

MARGARET BRENNAN  Since you want to restore public trust, tell me what you're doing now, because the Washington Post and Bloomberg reported the White House is preparing an executive order on vaccines and autism. What is it going to prescribe? What is it going to do? Why are we seeing another announcement here when I know you are launching research into a plethora of issues that are contributing factors potentially to autism. Why would the White House be saying only look at this thing?
DR. BHATTACHARYA: Well, I don't- I mean- I would have to ask the president about the specifics--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Because that is going to--
DR. BHATTACHARYA: --of the executive order. I tell you want we're doing--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Do you think that's restoring trust in vaccines?
DR. BHATTACHARYA: The- the purpose of the- whatever the- I mean I- you can ask the president about the executive order, but I'll tell you what the- the focus of the president has been--
MARGARET BRENNAN: You don't know about the executive order?

DR. BHATTACHARYA: I- I don't- I won't be able to tell you specifically what's on it because I don't think it's done yet. But you can ask the president about it. What I can tell you is that the president cares deeply, as does Bobby, about the rise in autism. I know you do as well. There's so many families around the country that- that have- that have had, you know, have faced the--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: --issues of this, right?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes, and they want real information.

DR. BHATTACHARYA: And so I, as NIH director, have been focused on making sure that we have science that addresses that- that very complicated question about why we've seen a rise in autism. It's not going to be a simple answer. And I- last year I authorized something called the Autism Data Science Initiative. We're going to have a big, sort of, early, sort of- sort of, results from it in a couple of weeks from the- the dozen and more scientific teams that have been funded to look at this, with a mandate of thinking very broadly, not just genes, not- not just environmental exposures, but potential interactions. We don't know- if you ask me as a scientist, do I know why we've seen this rise in autism? I'll tell you, I don't know the answer to that question.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

DR. BHATTACHARYA: And the fact that it gets so tied up with, okay, is it- is it vaccines? Not vaccines. It- what it does is it sends a signal to the scientists that if you work on this topic, you're going to get destroyed if you get the- the wrong answer.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

DR. BHATTACHARYA: I- I tried my hardest. The way you build public trust is allow people to talk and think without that kind of sort of political overlay. I've tried my very hardest as the NIH director to make- to allow that to happen--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Which is so key for science. Which is why I'm asking why the president putting out an order specifically focused on one, what seems to be preconceived notion, how that would--
DR. BHATTACHARYA: You're jumping ahead. I mean, I don't know exactly what's in this executive order and neither do you. So it's- it's not yet--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, it's- it's interesting that you don't. My colleague Matt Gutman here at CBS asked you last week whether you think vaccines cause autism. You said you don't know for certain. You said there isn't evidence that any vaccine causes autism, but you also don't have evidence that vaccines do not. Parents are preparing to send their kids back to school.
[CROSSTALK]
DR. BHATTACHARYA: Okay, so just- I just want to be very clear what I actually said.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Please be clear. Should parents trust that they can go vaccinate their kids when their doctor tells them to do so for them to go back to school?

DR. BHATTACHARYA: I think- I think that- that parents, for most kids, especially for the measles vaccines, the DTP, all the standard childhood vaccines, it's very important that parents vaccinate their kids. As far as can they feel confident sending back to schools, you know, I just- just to push back some, it was a tremendous mistake to cause parents to fear that- about sending their kids to school during the COVID pandemic. The kids were better off in school. We shouldn't be scaring public--
MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm talking about what people do now. It's August, about to be September, kids are going back to school--
[CROSSTALK]
DR. BHATTACHARYA: Yeah, but Margaret you're talking about the--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --not talking about 2020. I'm talking about 2026.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: --you're talking about- we're talking about the- why people have--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --clarity from the federal government--
DR. BHATTACHARYA: Okay just so we're clear--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --and the top health official--
DR. BHATTACHARYA: If you want clarity, let me give you some clarity.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Please.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: The reason why you have this problem of public trust is because what happened in 2020 has not yet been addressed--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Can these parents trust you and the recommendation that they should--
DR. BHATTACHARYA: Yeah, I think- I mean- the--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --go get their kids vaccinated?

DR. BHATTACHARYA: --the parents should be trusting me. I mean, I'm giving my recommendation. I vaccinated my kids. I don't think that it is a- I think if you want to protect your kids from these- these- these sort of preventable diseases, yes, you should vaccinate your kids. But it is even more important that these kids go to school. That in no way, shape, or form should this show or any other show like it perpetuate the idea that- that sending their kids to school is worse because there's going to be some health risk there when it's just not true, right? If you want to protect your kids from those- those preventable diseases, vaccinate your kids. I've been very, very clear about that. But it is- it is a mistake, and it contributes to the lack of public trust if you sort of fearmonger around, 'oh, if you send your kids to school, well, you might be around unvaccinated kids.' That's- that's a- that's a tremendous mistake, right? If you vaccinate your kids, you can protect your kids from those- those- those risks, whatever they are. In- in any case, it's better to send the kids to school because that's how you keep kids healthy.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes, we want to send our kids to school.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: So, but now addressing what happened in 2020 is part of that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: If you want to say why there's this loss of public trust, you have to really wrap your arms around that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you trust the science and the health workers and the vaccines now, is what I understood you were saying, and so that is the message that I think we can--
DR. BHATTACHARYA: I mean, I trust the science. I mean, I've looked at the scientific evidence--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --end on here.
DR. BHATTACHARYA: --and there's lots. I mean, I personally have made decisions for my family around those lines too, so--
MARGARET BRENNAN: That's good to know. Thank you. We're going to leave it there because I know we're running out of time. We'll be back in a moment.

title: Netanyahu rejects Gaza peace plan, vows no military withdrawal until Hamas disarms
summary: President Trump hailed the peace plan​ as a "historic agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and all other groups in Gaza."
story: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected a U.S.-backed Gaza peace plan and vowed there would be no military withdrawal until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.

Last month, President Trump hailed the peace plan as a "historic agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and all other groups in Gaza." He said it was negotiated by his international "Board of Peace" and called it a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security."
On Sunday, after more than a week of gradually escalating criticism of the plan, Netanyahu explicitly opposed it as he faced pushback from his right-wing base ahead of elections.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document," he said in a cabinet meeting, adding that the military "will not make any withdrawal until Hamas is truly disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens."

Under the plan, Israeli forces would withdraw from parts of Gaza as "disarmament is completed," Mr. Trump said in a Truth Social post on July 30, with an International Stabilization Force and a new Palestinian police force responsible for security.

"This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people," the president wrote. "At the same time, Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks."
Netanyahu, who has faced calls from his far-right allies to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan, said on Sunday that Israel is speaking with the U.S. about its objections.

"They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us, and we know how to stand up to these things," he said. "We have proven this in the past and we are proving it today. In addition, the IDF will continue to thwart threats against our forces and against our citizens."
Netanyahu said Hamas must give up all of its weapons, a goal that Board of Peace members say is not realistically achievable.
"We are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament," Netanyahu said.
In response to Netanyahu's remarks, Hamas said Sunday that it remains committed to the roadmap reached by the mediators and the Board of Peace.

"Our acceptance of the roadmap, despite all the challenges, reflected a sense of national responsibility upheld by the resistance factions, foremost among them Hamas, in consideration of the interests of the Palestinian people," said Bassem Naim, a member of the Hamas political bureau, adding that it expects mediators and the U.S. to pressure Netanyahu.

The negotiations stem from a 20-point peace proposal that Mr. Trump offered last fall to end the war between Israel and Hamas. The conflict broke out with Hamas' terrorist attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

title: 2,000-year-old Roman shipwreck discovered off coast of Sicily
summary: The discovery was made by an underwater fisherman who described it as the "most incredible" in his life.
story: Italian divers have discovered the 2,100-year-old wreck of a Roman ship off Sicily, piled high with hundreds of well-preserved ancient clay jars, known as amphorae, which were likely used to transport wine.

The wreck, dubbed by Italy's Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years", was found some three miles off the coast of Mazara del Vallo.

Divers from the cultural heritage protection arm of Palermo's police said Saturday they had located the ship, thought to date to between the 2nd and 1st centuries BC, some 150 feet down, after a tip-off from fishermen.

Scoperto al largo di Mazara del Vallo un relitto romano del II-I sec a.C., con centinaia di anfore.«Una delle più importanti scoperte archeologiche subacquee degli ultimi anni», dichiara il Min Giuli, congratulandosi con @_Carabinieri_ Nucleo TPC e SopMare della Regione Sicilia pic.twitter.com/H1JbfX8MzF

In an Instagram post, underwater fishermen Giacomo De Mola described seeing "something" on his boat's underwater scanner which resembled a rock. De Mola said he decided to dive and investigate anyway, when he stumbled upon what he described as "without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life."
"Visibility wasn't the best... I got closer. And my heart stopped. Below me was a vast expanse of amphorae," De Mola said in the instagram post, along with video footage of the discovery.
He said he "immediately" reported the discovery to the Superintendent of the sea of the Sicilian Region.
"It's hard to explain what it feels like to be among the first human beings, after almost twenty centuries, to see that place again," he said.
The ship, reported in local media to be some 21 metres long and six metres wide, was mostly carrying Dressel 1A amphorae, which were tall and cylindrical, and mainly used for carrying wine.

title: Prince William, Kate Middleton could seek 'gentleman's agreement' to protect Prince George at Eton: experts
summary: Royal experts say Prince George's dating life and school years at Eton College could test the limits of the British press agreement in the smartphone era.
story: Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," says Prince George passed Eton's admissions process like other applicants before accepting his place at the prestigious school.
Prince William and Kate Middleton could use a "gentleman's agreement" when Prince George starts Eton College in the fall — and it could face the ultimate test in the smartphone era.

GB News reported that the Prince and Princess of Wales could forge an agreement with the British press to limit intrusions into the life of their eldest son. Royal author and former broadcaster Simon Vigar told the outlet it’s the same approach that protected the early days of their romance at the University of St. Andrews.
Fox News Digital reached out to Kensington Palace for comment.
PRINCE WILLIAM AND KATE MIDDLETON 'CAUTIOUS' ABOUT WHICH ROYAL APPEARANCES THEIR CHILDREN MAKE: SOURCE
Prince George of Wales is said to be excited that he'll be attending Eton College in the fall. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Prince William and Princess Catherine are realistic enough to know that they cannot completely control the environment around Prince George," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. "Most people have a camera in their pocket now, and one photograph can be online and around the world before the palace even knows it exists."

"What they can do is establish very clear boundaries with the British press," she said. "There is a huge difference between legitimate coverage of Prince George carrying out public engagements and somebody photographing a teenager going about his public life at school. The palace cannot police every teenager with an iPhone, but the press can make a conscious decision not to create a market for those intrusive photographs."

Catherine, Princess of Wales, Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Prince George attended the 2026 Easter Matins Service at St. George's Chapel in Windsor, England, on April 5, 2026. (Mark Cuthbert/UK Press/Getty Images)
In June, Kensington Palace announced that George, who turned 13 on July 22, would attend the prestigious boarding school where his father and uncle, Prince Harry, were educated.
WATCH: PRINCE GEORGE EARNED ETON COLLEGE SPOT WITH NO SPECIAL TREATMENT: EXPERT

Eton College, founded in 1440 by King Henry VI, has educated generations of leaders, including 20 British prime ministers. George, who is second in line to the throne, will likely meet many of his future peers there.
British royals expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that the "new age" of smartphones and social media is one of the many reasons Eton College is chosen "among the elites."

Students from Eton College in the Mound Stand react to Harrow students during a cricket match between Eton and Harrow at Lord's Cricket Ground in London, England, on May 10, 2024. (Philip Brown/Getty Images)

"Many classmates are from extremely wealthy and well-connected families," she said. "Within this circle are unwritten rules of conduct. Throwing a pupil to the media risks being ostracized from the inner circles."
A view of Eton College founded by King Henry VI. (Archive Photos/Getty Images)
Eton College is known for fiercely protecting its students from prying eyes, creating a world within its walls where they can simply be pupils.
"For Prince George and every high-profile teenager, everything could become international news within minutes," royal broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital.
Boys make their way to classes at Eton College, date unknown. (Christopher Furlong/Getty Images)

"We're in a better place," she said. "Years ago, after Princess Diana's death, I believe Prince William and Prince Harry forced positive change. The old paparazzi harassment was replaced with something somewhat controlled and truce-like."

When William and Harry were in school, an informal agreement was reached between the palace and the British press: As long as the brothers were pursuing their studies, their privacy was to be respected, Vanity Fair reported.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Prince William signs in on his first day at Eton College on Sept. 6, 1995. (Anwar Hussein/WireImage)
According to the outlet, this media truce allowed William and Kate to quietly build their relationship outside the public eye when they were students.
Prince William stands at Eton College in Eton, United Kingdom, wearing a waistcoat as a member of the elite prefect society called "Pop." (Tim Graham/Photo Library via Getty Images)

William and Kate met in 2001 at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. They were close friends before they began dating more than a year later. Their romance remained a secret for nearly two years before becoming public. That level of discretion, Vanity Fair reported, was made possible, in part, by the informal agreement with the press.
The couple married in 2011.
Kate Middleton is seen waving to members of the public during a visit to the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, on Feb. 25, 2011. (CARL DE SOUZA/AFP via Getty Images)

Vigar told GB News that William and Kate want to offer the same level of privacy to their three children. Their children's first romantic relationships as they grow older "are already the subject of careful consideration," according to Vanity Fair. If the press respects George's privacy while he's in school, it could set a precedent for his siblings, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis, to enjoy the same discretion.

"The 'gentleman's agreement' is more than necessary now," said Chard. "Prince William knows firsthand what privacy during school gave him. This handshake is perceived as a little fragile now and not necessary due to traditional paparazzi. Friends at school with their smartphones can become instant paparazzi."
A young Prince Harry is seen here at Eton College. (Tim Graham/Getty Images)

"George will have mentors, both family and at school, to guide him through pitfalls. No one wants him to feel burdened at 13. He should have space to grow, to be with friends, to be pain-free at Eton."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

The Prince and Princess of Wales, seen here on the Isle of Mull, western Scotland, on April 30, 2025, have agreed that their eldest, Prince George, will attend Eton College. (Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images)
The Prince and Princess of Wales are also navigating what it's like to raise a teenager.
During the Commonwealth Games in Scotland, cycling champion Laura Kenny invited the couple to "come and give it a go" on a tandem bike, The Telegraph reported.
Princess Catherine and Prince George attend the men's singles final at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club in London, England, circa 2022. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)
When Welsh TV presenter Gethin Jones asked the royal children if they would like to see their parents "on a tandem in the velodrome," George quickly said, "No."
Prince George is seen here with his younger sister Princess Charlotte in London on July 12, 2026. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)
"We embarrass you enough as it is," said William.
When the royal family received their own Welsh cycling outfits, William joked, "You know me, Lycra!"

Catherine, Princess of Wales, Prince William and Dame Laura Kenny watch track cycling during the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome on Aug. 1, 2026, in Glasgow, Scotland. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
"I won't whip the shorts out," the prince promised.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

Prince George of Wales, wearing a hat and sunglasses, attends Day 14 of the Wimbledon Tennis Championships at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club in London, on July 12, 2026. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)
Royal experts told Fox News Digital that the privacy challenge could become more complicated when George starts dating.

"George understands why people are interested in him," said Schofield. "A teenage girlfriend may find herself facing international attention simply because she sat next to him or was photographed leaving the same place. But Prince William will remember exactly what Catherine experienced. Her family, her friendships, her background and, eventually, almost every aspect of her life became subjects of enormous public interest."
Prince George of Wales attends Trooping the Colour on June 13, 2026, in London. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

"I would expect William and Catherine to be fiercely protective when the day comes," said Schofield. "Especially while George and whoever he's dating are still minors. And I think the media has to exercise some common sense. A teenage romance involving Prince George is not automatically a royal courtship. Hopefully, we will all give him that space."

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Catherine, Princess of Wales, Princess Charlotte, Prince George and Prince Louis watch an RAF flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace after attending Trooping the Colour 2026 on June 13, 2026, in London. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital it's also likely William will remind his eldest son not to cause "mischief" while at Eton.
"George has been very family friendly, so I don't envision major changes in the dynamics," said Turner. "He must remember William knows every trick in the book."

Prince George of Wales and King Charles III watch an RAF flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace following the coronation of King Charles III and Queen Camilla at Westminster Abbey on May 6, 2023, in London. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Eton was also picked due to its proximity to their home at Windsor," Fordwich pointed out. "Prince William credits his afternoon teas with his beloved grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, on Sundays. It was just a short walk from Eton. George will likely stay close to both his parents and spend time with them."
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON FINALLY FEEL FREE TO SHOW AFFECTION IN PUBLIC: EXPERTS

Prince George of Wales watches an RAF flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace after the coronation of King Charles III and Queen Camilla at Westminster Abbey in London, circa 2023. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
Schofield told Fox News Digital that the Prince and Princess of Wales are determined to let George enjoy his school years and make new friends in private, without the added pressures of royal life.

"Teenagers naturally want independence," said Schofield. "Prince George is going to want to make his own decisions and develop interests that have nothing to do with becoming king. At the same time, public curiosity about him is only going to increase.

Prince George of Wales and Prince Louis of Wales stand during Trooping the Colour on June 13, 2026, in London, England. Trooping the Colour is a ceremonial parade celebrating the official birthday of the British monarch. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)

"These years could be enormously important in shaping the king he eventually becomes. William and Catherine had introduced royal life gradually rather than overwhelming him with it. We've seen George at family engagements, but he has still been allowed to be a schoolboy first."

Prince George and Prince William are seen at the UEFA Champions League quarterfinal match between Paris Saint-Germain and Aston Villa at Parc des Princes in Paris on April 9, 2025. (Pierre Suu/Getty Images)

"The goal shouldn't be to manufacture the perfect future king at 13," she continued. "It should be to produce a confident, grounded adult who understands the institution but has also experienced enough of ordinary life to understand the people he will one day serve. Giving Prince George a genuine adolescence could ultimately be one of the best preparations for kingship William and Catherine can give him."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

story: Fox News contributor Tammy Bruce joins Rachel Campos-Duffy to recap this week’s pop culture news on ‘Fox & Friends Weekend.’

Jessica Alba showed off an animal-print bikini while sharing highlights from her summer on social media. (Jessica Alba/Instagram)

Jessica Alba hit the golf course with a friend while sharing highlights from her August activities. (Jessica Alba/Instagram)

MOLLY SIMS FLAUNTS TONED ABS IN MISMATCHED BIKINI DURING PERFECT BEACH DAY WITH HER KIDS

The actress has previously spoken about how her understanding of love has changed over time.

"Over time, I’ve learned to embrace every version of how love can show up," Alba told Elle in May. "Love shows up in so many different ways, and it’s not always grand gestures. Sometimes it’s just holding space."

"It’s not always a movie or a rom-com," she told the outlet. "Sometimes love is just sitting there when someone’s not feeling well and rubbing their head, or just allowing someone to rage and giving them space. But still being there and knowing that nothing they can do can push you away."
MARTHA STEWART GETS CANDID ABOUT PLASTIC SURGERY, DATING AS SHE TURNS 85

title: Brad Pitt admits he began drinking again after years of sobriety
summary: Brad Pitt tells Esquire he got "back off the wagon" after seven years sober and describes the one period he says he understood suicide as relief.
story: Jon Voight spoke to Fox News Digital while promoting his film "Reagan," and weighed in on the family drama between his daughter Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt.
After seven years of sobriety, Brad Pitt started drinking again.
The startling confession came as Pitt reflected on his darkest moments, the lasting scars of grief and the complicated reality of struggling despite having "won the lottery" in life.
"I was sober for seven years. And then I got back off the wagon," Pitt told Esquire for the September cover story.
COUNTRY SINGER RUSTON KELLY COMMITS TO SOBRIETY AFTER RELAPSING ON DRUGS FOLLOWING FREAK GOLF CART CRASH
Brad Pitt revealed he started drinking again after seven years of sobriety in a candid new interview. (Samir Hussein/WireImage))

The actor said he approached drinking differently after giving up his sobriety, describing his consumption as more limited than before. "In a more restrained manner," he clarified. "I got overconfident a couple times, went, ‘Yep, nope, not good for me. Not in big quantities.’"

Pitt’s candid admission came as he reflected on the harder chapters of his life and acknowledged that fame and success had not insulated him from struggle. The "F1" star has been dealing with "family stuff" since 2016, when he began the divorce process from his ex-wife, Angelina Jolie.
Pitt’s reflections took a darker turn as he recalled a period when the pain became nearly unbearable.

"I was never suicidal in any way. It just was not my makeup," he told the outlet. "In fact, if I have any afflictions, it’s probably being a congenital optimist. Which has helped many times, and it’s also gotten me – I’ve walked foolishly head-on into a Mack truck because of my optimism. Or, as my forever-funny friend David Fincher will say, 'Yeah, you see the glass as half full, but it’s half full of urine.' Anyway, I’ve never been suicidal except for one little period."
Brad Pitt reflected on sobriety, grief and the difficult years dealing with "family stuff." (CHANTAL ANDERSON/Esquire)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"And in that one little period, I just thought – I just couldn’t – just didn’t see a way out," Pitt continued. "The pain was so oppressive that – I wasn’t going to act on this, but I could feel – I could feel the cold steel of the bullet in my head, and it felt like relief. And I thought, Oh, okay, now I understand – I understand suicide, in the sense that it’s just relief. It’s just looking for relief from the pain. But I also think we have incredible survival instincts. And for me, that immediately kicked in, but it was just... "
The Oscar winner tempered his candid admission by acknowledging the extraordinary hand he had been dealt in life.
Brad Pitt said fame and success did not shield him from personal struggles. (CHANTAL ANDERSON/Esquire)
"Yeah. Like, listen: This s--t ain’t easy," he said. "And you’re talking to a guy who won the lottery."
Pitt also reflected on the lasting impact of grief, describing the pain it left behind alongside an unexpected sense of beauty.
"Grief, if you survive it, leaves a gaping hole, but it also leaves profound beauty," he said. "It’s an aching beauty, but it’s beauty."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Brad Pitt poses for the cover of Esquire magazine. (CHANTAL ANDERSON/Esquire)

Pitt first gained major attention with his memorable supporting turn in 1991’s "Thelma & Louise," before becoming a leading man in films including "A River Runs Through It," "Legends of the Fall" and "Se7en."
His signature films include "Fight Club," "Ocean’s Eleven," "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button," "Moneyball" and "Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood."
Brad Pitt smiling in a scene from the film 'Thelma & Louise', 1991. (Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer/Getty Images)

Pitt has also built an influential career behind the camera through his production company, Plan B Entertainment. As a producer, he won the best picture Oscar for "12 Years a Slave," adding to a résumé that extends well beyond acting.
Now in his 60s, Pitt looked back on the previous decade with a sense of urgency.
"God, I want my fifties back," he said. "I would do more. Your fifties are just – man, anything that’s on your mind, go. Go attack it. Go attack it now."

title: Ben Jones, 'Dukes of Hazzard' actor and former congressman, dead at 84
summary: Ben Jones, who played mechanic Cooter Davenport on "The Dukes of Hazzard," died from a heart attack at age 84, his wife announced.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
"The Dukes of Hazzard" star Ben Jones has died. He was 84.
The actor appeared as "good ol' boy" mechanic Cooter Davenport in the beloved series from 1979 to 1985.

Jones had a "massive heart attack" at his home Sunday in Washington, Virginia, as he was waiting to watch his beloved Atlanta Braves play baseball, his wife, Alma Viator, said on social media. The couple had been married since 1992.
Rappahannock County Sheriff Connie Compton also confirmed his death.
Ben Jones died at age 84 after a heart attack, according to his wife. (CBS via Getty Images)

Viator wrote on Facebook, "I lost the love of my life today. Ben passed from a massive heart attack. He was home resting in his favorite chair waiting for the Braves to come on and whoop the Yankees."
"Ben had the most amazing rich full life. He loved and was loved by so many. He will be missed. I love him so so much," she finished off her post.
Viator shared the news along with an image of Ben holding a dog.
Jones was born in Edgecombe County, North Carolina on August 30, 1941.
‘KNOTS LANDING’ STAR DONNA MILLS SAYS REFUSING TO POSE NUDE COST HER PLAYBOY COVER

Cast members from "The Dukes of Hazzard" pose for a group photo in Los Angeles on Jan. 1. Front row, from left: Rick Hurst, John Schneider, Catherine Bach, Tom Wopat and James Best, with basset hound Sandy. Back row, from left: Sorrell Booke, Denver Pyle and Ben Jones. (CBS via Getty Images)
He got his start on stage, before making his film debut in 1972 for "Together For Days" as Douglas. He also appeared in "Moonrunners" in 1975 as Fred and "The Lincoln Conspiracy" in 1977.
On the TV front, Jones made his television debut in 1976, playing a thief in an episode of "Movin’ On."
He also appeared in the 1977 series "Nashville 99," and "The Magical World of Disney" in 1978.
Jones landed the role of Cooter Davenport in "The Dukes of Hazzard" in the seventies.
‘DALLAS' STAR LINDA GRAY REVEALS THE BIZARRE WAY LARRY HAGMAN AVOIDED KISSING SCENES
Ben Jones played Cooter Davenport on "Dukes of Hazzard." (Rick Diamond/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
He played Davenport for more than 140 episodes from 1979 to 1985.
He reprised his role as Davenport in "The Dukes of Hazzard: Reunion!" in 1997 and "The Dukes of Hazzard: Hazzard in Hollywood" in 2000.
His final TV appearance was in "Surface" in 2005, and his final film he appeared in was the 2021 movie "Unbreakable."
In addition to his acting career, Jones also had a political career.
ANN-MARGRET, 85, REVEALS THE HABIT THAT KEEPS HER FEELING FOREVER YOUNG

James Best as Rosco P. Coltrane, Rick Hurst as Deputy Cletus Hogg, Tom Wopat as Luke Duke, Catherine Bach as Daisy Duke, John Schneider as Bo Duke and Ben Jones as Cooter Davenport pose together in the made-for-television movie ‘The Dukes of Hazzard: Reunion!’ air date April 25, 1997. (CBS via Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Jones served two terms in the House of Representatives.
He served as a U.S. House of Representatives member from Georgia’s fourth district from 1989 until 1993.
Jones’ "Dukes of Hazzard" co-star Tom Wopat shared a statement to Fox News Digital, and also shared it on his Instagram on Sunday.
The Dukes of Hazzard" cast members Tom Wopat with co-stars Catherine Bach and John Schneider in 1981. (CBS via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Wopat, who played Lucas K. "Luke" Duke, said: "’The Dukes of Hazzard’ lost another integral part of their cast today. Ben Jones was a fine friend and a fierce advocate of all the best things we can offer in the entertainment business. He will be sorely missed… Denver Pyle frequently said to Ben, ‘I’m not your Uncle Jesse!’ But I feel like we lost a Duke cousin today."

Whey Jennings, grandson of country music legend Waylon Jennings, is also grieving the loss of his dear friend and musical supporter. The two shared the stage on multiple occasions, but their bond extended well beyond performing together. Jones also helped finance Jennings’ first recorded live album, playing a meaningful role in the singer-songwriter’s career.
Whey Jennings (right), Waylon Jennings' grandson, is seen here with Ben Jones (center) and his wife Alma Viator. (Courtesy of Whey Jennings)

"Wow, this one hurts," Jennings told Fox News Digital. "I'll never forget all you have done for me, brother. It's been an honor to share the stage with you so many times. Thank you for believing in me. You have been a true friend when I needed one most, and I'm gonna miss you so much. I love you, Ben. Alma, I love you very much. Big hugs and prayers."
The show and Cooter lived on because it was funny, had plenty of action and car chases and had a good, family-friendly heart, Jones previously told the Richmond Times-Dispatch in 2001.
"The show reflects the values of the heartland of America. The good guys always win," Jones said.
The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Prince William was 'fuming' over request for Kate Middleton to spell her name differently: book
summary: King Charles III and Queen Camilla allegedly asked Kate Middleton to change her name spelling over royal crest concerns, leaving Prince William fuming.
story: Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," tells Fox News Digital that the Princess of Wales’ modern approach, family values and "soft power" make her a vital asset to the royal family and the UK.

Prince William was reportedly "fuming" after King Charles III and Queen Camilla suggested that Kate Middleton change the spelling of her first name when she joined the royal family, according to a new book.

"Charles and Camilla each had a royal monogram that consisted of interlocking C’s beneath a crown, and they expressed concern that a third royal cypher with a C was overkill," Christopher Andersen wrote in his biography "Kate! The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen." "Would Kate mind if she changed the spelling of her full name from ‘Catherine’ to ‘Katherine.’"

Andersen added, "Offended by yet another command from on high essentially aimed at placating Camilla, a fuming William replied on his wife’s behalf. The request was nothing less than ‘insulting,’ he told his father, not only to Kate but to her entire family."
KATE MIDDLETON IS 'INDISPENSABLE' TO ROYAL FAMILY AS SLIMMED-DOWN MONARCHY FACES MOUNTING PRESSURE: EXPERT
Prince William was "fuming" after then-Prince Charles asked if Kate Middleton would change her name from Catherine to Katherine, according to a new book. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
A Kensington Palace spokesperson told Fox News Digital they don't comment on books.

"The entire nature of Charles and Camilla's request — that Catherine was adding too many C's to the royal crests — shows just how much image and branding means to members of the royal family. The monarchy really is a giant game of one-upmanship," Andersen told Fox News Digital, adding that from the very beginning of their relationship "William has gone to war for Kate."
William’s top concern has always been for the Princess of Wales’ "safety," but he also came out "guns blazing" in her defense after topless photos of her sunbathing were published in France in 2012.

"He angrily ordered Palace lawyers to sue and even wanted to see those involved prosecuted criminally under French privacy laws," Andersen said. "When they started a family, it was William who made sure that Kate was not forced to take on too heavy a royal workload if it meant that she would have to spend too much time away from their children."
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON FINALLY FEEL FREE TO SHOW AFFECTION IN PUBLIC: EXPERTS

But, he said the king and Camilla "expected her to go along because she has always been a nice, cooperative team player … but didn't take into account the fact that she personally prefers to be known as Catherine and feels very strongly about the name her parents gave her."
While most of the world knows her by her nickname, Kate, her real name is Catherine.
The princess is "genuinely fond" of Charles and assumed that he got the "absurd" idea from someone else, Andersen explained, adding that she didn’t hold any ill will toward him.
Prince William has "gone to war for Kate" since the beginning of their relationship, royal author Christopher Andersen said. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
"Besides, it wasn't long before they were having to deal with their simultaneous cancer diagnoses, which put everything else in stark perspective," he added.
KING CHARLES CONSIDERED QUEEN CAMILLA 'NON-NEGOTIABLE' AFTER PRINCESS DIANA, AUTHOR CLAIMS
"Kate!: The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen" by Christopher Andersen is available now. (Gallery Books)
And although Middleton comes off as "kind and compassionate," she still has a "will of steel," he said.

"Kate is very secure about who she is and how she wants to be perceived by the outside world," Andersen said. "Changing her formal given name for such a bizarre, almost comical reason was a bridge too far."

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard called the issue a "nonstarter" and a "lost cause," telling Fox News Digital that Charles and Camilla were thinking with a "business head" since she was known to the world as Kate anyway.
"Although a hopeless endeavour, I can see both sides of the coin," she admitted, explaining that William was not only offended for his wife but for his in-laws as well.
PRINCE WILLIAM REFUSES TO QUIT HOBBY THAT TERRIFIES KATE MIDDLETON: EXPERTS
King Charles III, Queen Camilla, Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Kate Middleton pose for a photograph at Buckingham Palace in 2023. (Getty Images)
But "the concerns were brushed aside. It wasn’t important enough to cause a fight. They had bigger fish to fry."

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner called it a possible "volatile moment" between Camilla and the princess as she joined the family, "but nowadays, William was there to protect her. Since then, Kate has managed to stay one step behind when Charles and Camilla are around so as not to outstage them."
KING CHARLES SENDS 'DEFIANCE' MESSAGE TO PRINCE WILLIAM WITH BUCKINGHAM PALACE ROOM OFFER TO HARRY: EXPERT
He noted, however, that more recently the 44-year-old is "building a stronger brand in her own right as William tries to take on the reins of Kingmanship."
"If true, it’s idiotic," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital of the story. "The idea is simply stupid. And why? Because her name began with C and theirs did!"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Andersen also felt the incident "speaks volumes about how conscious the royals are of all the bells and whistles — not just the gold coaches, the castles, and the crown jewels, but things as small as the letters in their crests and coats of arms. It may seem trivial to the rest of us, but to them things like this mean everything."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Joan Jett cancels remaining 2026 concerts after undergoing surgery for 'fractured vertebrae'
summary: Joan Jett underwent orthopedic surgery on a fractured vertebrae, forcing cancellation of her September shows including Bourbon & Beyond festival.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel breaks down the symptoms of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus amid music legend Billy Joels brain diagnosis and why its under-diagnosed on Fox Report.
Joan Jett is stepping away from the stage after suffering a serious injury that required surgery.

In a since-expired post shared to Jett's Instagram Story on Tuesday, the 67-year-old rock icon's team announced that her band Joan Jett & the Blackhearts had canceled their two remaining scheduled 2026 concerts in September.
"Following a recent injury, Joan Jett has undergone orthopedic surgery on a fractured vertebrae and will begin the necessary healing process," the statement read, via Rolling Stone.
Joan Jett is taking a break from performing after undergoing surgery following a "recent injury." (Getty Images for Janie's Fund)
JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY ENDS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN SHOW AFTER HEALTH SETBACK

"In close consultation with her doctors, Joan will not be able to perform at her forthcoming September scheduled shows in Costa Mesa, California, on Sept. 5 and Louisville, Kentucky, on Sept. 24," it continued.
"While Joan hates to disappoint fans, she will be taking this time to focus on physical therapy and healing. She's looking forward to delivering tremendous concerts for many years to come."
No additional details about Jett's injury were provided. Fox News Digital has reached out to Jett's representatives for comment.
The 67-year-old singer canceled her remaining two scheduled concerts for 2026.  (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images for The Michael J. Fox Foundation)
The Pacific Amphitheatre in Costa Mesa, where the singer was set to perform on Sept. 5, shared Jett's statement on their webpage along with an update.
KACEY MUSGRAVES ABRUPTLY CANCELS CONCERT DATES FROM 'MIDDLE OF NOWHERE' TOUR
"While we understand this is a disappointment to all of you, we are happy to announce that Cheap Trick will be performing in her place, with X opening the show," the statement read.
"If you wish to attend the Cheap Trick / X show on Sept. 5, do nothing and your tickets will be valid. We look forward to seeing you," it added.
"If you wish to get a refund, please contact your point of purchase and we hope to see you at another show in the future."

Jett's concert in Louisville was scheduled to take place on the opening day of the four-day Bourbon & Beyond festival at the Highland Festival Grounds at the Kentucky Exposition Center. The festival's lineup includes Foo Fighters, Queens of the Stone Age, Mumford & Sons, Chris Stapleton, Kacey Musgraves and others.
Jett rose to international stardom after founding Joan Jett & the Blackhearts in 1979.  (Reuters)
Jett first rose to fame in the 1970s as a founding member of the all-female rock band The Runaways. She later found international success after she founded Joan Jett & the Blackhearts in 1979.

The band released 10 albums between 1981 and 2013, scoring major hits including "I Love Rock ’n Roll," "Bad Reputation" and "I Hate Myself for Loving You." Joan Jett and the Blackhearts were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2015.
In 2022, Joan Jett & the Blackhearts released their first acoustic album, "Changeup," followed by their six-song EP "Mindsets" in 2023.

Joan Jett & the Blackhearts have stayed active on the road since they first formed. In recent years, they have toured alongside artists including Def Leppard, Mötley Crüe, Bryan Adams, Alanis Morissette and Billy Idol. The band completed their first U.K. headline tour in 16 years in July.

title: 'Highlander' star Christopher Lambert hospitalized after collapsing at Steel City Con
summary: Christopher Lambert collapsed at Steel City Con reportedly due to low blood sugar and dehydration, but a representative says the actor is "perfectly OK."
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
"Highlander" star Christopher Lambert suffered a medical scare after collapsing at Steel City Con in Philadelphia during a meet and greet over the weekend.
The 69-year-old had to leave the convention due to a "personal issue," according to the event's Facebook page.
The French actor was subsequently taken to a local hospital by ambulance, according to TMZ.
Christopher Lambert collapsed at Steel City Con in Philadelphia on Saturday. (Getty Images)

A representative for Lambert told TMZ that the actor was "perfectly OK" and resting at his hotel. The representative said Lambert had not gotten enough sleep the previous night and had eaten little during the day, causing his blood sugar to drop.
Steel City Con representatives told People that the actor had become overheated and dehydrated.

"Christopher was feeling a little overheated and dehydrated. He had to sit down, but he is doing great today," organizers told the outlet.

The convention said Lambert was expected to return Sunday for scheduled photo opportunities and a noon Q&A panel. Steel City Con’s official schedule lists Lambert as appearing Friday, Saturday and Sunday during the Aug. 7-9 event.

Lambert is best known for starring as immortal swordsman Connor MacLeod in the 1986 cult classic "Highlander." He also portrayed Tarzan in 1984’s "Greystoke: The Legend of Tarzan, Lord of the Apes" and Lord Raiden in the 1995 film adaptation of "Mortal Kombat."

story: "Free Bert" star Bert Kreischer reflects on his weight-loss journey, sobriety and a series of life-changing events that gave him a new perspective on mortality.
John Goodman is turning heads with his dramatic transformation.
The 74-year-old actor appeared nearly unrecognizable in a new photo with fellow actor David DeLuise after the two unexpectedly crossed paths at a grocery store.
DeLuise, known for playing Jerry Russo on Disney Channel's "Wizards of Waverly Place," shared the snapshot on Instagram Thursday, showing himself smiling alongside a noticeably slimmer Goodman.

John Goodman looks unrecognizable in a new photo amid his weight-loss journey. (Getty Images; daviddeluise/Instagram)
"He was my childhood!! Legend!" DeLuise wrote in the caption. "I love that I get to say that to someone ;), if you know you know."
Goodman's latest appearance comes after the "Roseanne" star spent years shifting his lifestyle and shedding a significant amount of weight.

The veteran actor previously revealed that he was approaching 400 pounds at his heaviest and had struggled for years with losing weight, only to gain it back.
In 2010, Goodman revealed that he had lost more than 100 pounds after cutting sugar from his diet and committing to regular exercise, including working out six days a week.

Goodman turned to boxing and daily walks as his form of movement.

"I dug it. Yeah. Nobody’s going to get hurt, but it’s just hitting the mitts and trying to learn," he told The Rolling Stone in 2023. "I never got good enough where I would trust myself to spar because once I get whacked in the face, I don’t know if I wouldn’t lose it."

title: 'Dallas' star Linda Gray reveals the bizarre way Larry Hagman avoided kissing scenes
summary: Linda Gray, who starred as Sue Ellen Ewing, shares wild stories from the "Dallas" set, including Patrick Duffy's surprise ambush and Larry Hagman's on-set pranks.
story: The actor, who was a sex symbol in the '80s, recalled playing the love interest of Brooke Shields and Linda Gray. Atkins now wants to work behind-the-scenes as a filmmaker.
Linda Gray is ready to kiss and tell.

The actress, who played Sue Ellen Ewing, the glamorous, famously troubled wife of villain J.R. Ewing on "Dallas," is teaming up with Julien's Auctions for "Ladies of the '80s," which goes live Aug. 12.

The sale gives bidders the chance to own costumes, props, personal archives and other rare memorabilia from some of the decade's most beloved television stars. It features two of Gray's original "Dallas" scripts from the episodes surrounding the infamous "Who Shot J.R.?" saga.
ANN-MARGRET, 85, REVEALS THE HABIT THAT KEEPS HER FEELING FOREVER YOUNG
"Dallas" aired from April 2, 1978, to May 3, 1991. At its peak in the 1980s, it was one of the biggest shows on television, (CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images)
Ahead of the auction, Gray looked back on her "Dallas" years, including the less-than-romantic kissing scenes she shared with her on-screen husband, Larry Hagman, who died in 2012 at 81.

"The first time we kissed, he had a mouthful of peanut butter," the actress told Fox News Digital. "I thought, 'Oh no.' And I had to keep going with this kiss. The camera didn't know what was going on. But here I was, kissing him with peanut butter. I almost killed him. I was like, 'You are so bad and very inappropriate, Larry.' And he didn't care. He just kept laughing. He thought that was funny."
Linda Gray told Fox News Digital that Larry Hagman wasn't a fan of filming kissing scenes. He'd often pull silly pranks to ease the awkwardness and keep everyone laughing. (CBS/Getty Images)

"And then it was onions," said the 85-year-old. "It was kissing him with peanut butter, onions, whatever he could find in a jar. That wasn't some romantic thing. On camera, it looked pretty good, but that was not my reality."
WATCH: CHRISTOPHER ATKINS LOOKS BACK AT ‘THE BLUE LAGOON’ AND ‘DALLAS’
Gray later discovered that Hagman wasn't a fan of on-screen kisses. Rather than endure the awkward moments, he turned them into practical jokes.
Larry Hagman died on Nov. 23, 2012, at the age of 81 in Dallas. (Gregg DeGuire/WireImage)

"He had told me quite honestly that he didn't like kissing scenes," said Gray. "And I thought, 'Well, we're going to be kissing a lot!' So when there was a kissing scene, Larry cringed, just cringed. He did not like it. But I think the pranks, psychologically, were his way of getting over the anxiety of having to kiss me on camera."
The "Dallas" set was notorious for its practical jokes, and everyone got caught in the crossfire.

Linda Gray (right, seen here with Larry Hagman) is offering treasures from her personal collection in Julien's Auctions' "Ladies of the '80s," featuring screen-used scripts, director's clapperboards, cast photos, awards, and more from her iconic career. Bidding is open now, with the live online auction taking place on Aug. 12, 2026. (Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images)

"It was a daily prank, if you can imagine," said Gray. "And you never knew who it was going to come from. But it was mainly Larry. Larry was the prankster. I remember there was one episode where Sue Ellen was in the hospital. I was attached to all kinds of tubes and things on my wrists, arms and nose — all this hospital stuff. Larry came in, and he was supposed to talk to Sue Ellen. And Sue Ellen was out of it. She wasn't speaking, which was great for me."
Linda Gray's personalized director's chair, used while directing episodes of "Dallas," is estimated to sell for $800–$1,200. (Julien's Auctions)

"So Larry sits beside my bed and starts telling Sue Ellen how much he loves her," she shared. "Very soap opera dialogue. He's going, 'Oh, Sue Ellen!' and I'm lying there with my eyes closed, my eyes rolling underneath my eyelids. Then the door opens again. I thought, 'Who is in this scene that I didn't know about?' It's Patrick Duffy. He stands next to Larry and says, 'I did not know this was in the scene. Would it help if we sang that old song we used to sing?' Larry says, 'Yes.' And then the two of them started singing this very inappropriate song. I can't even repeat the words to you."
An original drawing created by Tony Bennett for Linda Gray is estimated to sell for $300–$500. (Julien's Auctions)

"I just burst out laughing," she continued. "The tube came flying out of my nose. I was totally blindsided. I thought I had ruined the scene, but everyone just started laughing hysterically. That was just how it was every day."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

From left: Patrick Duffy, Linda Gray and Larry Hagman pose during the 18th annual Screen Actors Guild Awards broadcast at The Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles on Jan. 29, 2012. (Kevin Mazur/WireImage)
Hagman's practical jokes were one thing. Facing Texas women in real life was another altogether.

"I was at a Dallas hotel for an event," she recalled. "I went to the ladies' room to put on lipstick. Next to me was this lovely lady with a little Judith Leiber bag. She opened it to put on her lipstick. I glanced down, and there was a gun in her purse. That was all she had in it: a gun and lipstick. I thought, 'Oh boy, I'm in Texas. Who carries a gun around?' So I said, 'Excuse me, is that a gun?' Really stupid, I know. She said, 'Of course, darling. This is Texas!'"

From left: Charlene Tilton, Linda Gray, Larry Hagman, Patrick Duffy and Sheree J. Wilson won the TV Land Pop Culture Award for "Dallas." An award presented to Gray is estimated to sell for $500–$700. (L. Cohen/WireImage)

"I had never been to Dallas in my life," she reflected. "I remember landing in Texas. Everything was beige and flat. I thought, 'I've got to know the women here.' And where do the wealthy women of Texas go? Neiman Marcus, of course, to get their hair done. And that's what I did. I remember seeing big, big hair. It was unlike anything I saw in California. These women dressed a certain way. Their shoes were always very stylish. And apparently, they carried guns in their tiny evening bags."
In "Dallas," Linda Gray starred as Sue Ellen Ewing, the glamorous, resilient and unforgettable wife of J.R. Ewing (Larry Hagman) on the hit CBS series Dallas. (CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images)
Gray got a crash course in Texas high society over one unforgettable lunch.

"One woman invited me to lunch, and she wore a special outfit just for it," said Gray. "I didn't have any friends in California who would do that. We're having lunch, and then she looks at her watch. She says, 'Oh, I'm so sorry. I have to go home. I have to fluff and fold.' I'm thinking, 'She has to do laundry? Fluff her towels and fold them?' No. She had to fluff her hair, put on her makeup and turn into the woman her husband expected."
Two of Linda Gray's original *Dallas* scripts from the iconic "Who Shot J.R.?" storyline are estimated to sell for $300–$500. (Julien's Auctions)
If learning Texas customs was intimidating, keeping the show's biggest twist under wraps was downright terrifying.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Linda Gray arrives at the Larry Hagman and Linda Gray VIP Preview Party at Julien's Auction on June 1, 2011, in Beverly Hills. (Tibrina Hobson/WireImage)

The "Dallas" Season 3 finale ended with one of television's most famous cliffhangers: J.R. was shot by an unseen gunman, leaving viewers to wait eight months to learn not only who pulled the trigger but whether he survived.

Gray recalled that the writers were searching for a jaw-dropping way to end the season with a bang when one of them blurted out, "Let's just shoot the bastard." After a brief silence, everyone agreed: "What a great idea. We'll shoot him."

Linda Gray is seen here as Sue Ellen Ewing in a scene from "Dallas." The Ewing family returned to primetime in 2012 when "Dallas" was revived on TNT. After three seasons, the reboot concluded in 2014. (United Archives via Getty Images)
As "Who Shot J.R.?" became a worldwide obsession, Gray found herself fielding the question everywhere she went, including during an interview with David Hartman.

In the "Dallas" Season 3 finale, "A House Divided," J.R. Ewing (Larry Hagman) is gunned down by a mysterious assailant, setting off the legendary "Who Shot J.R.?" cliffhanger. The mystery captivated millions of viewers and became one of the biggest pop culture moments in television history. (© Lorimar Film Entertainment/Courtesy Everett Collection)

"I was not very smart, but I said, 'Yes, I do,'" Gray recalled when asked whether she knew the shooter's identity. "'I know, and one of my children knows.' After that, I thought, 'Oh my God, I just opened Pandora's box. I thought everyone was going to call my house and one of my kids would answer the phone and reveal who it was. And then it would be all over.'"
The moment the interview ended, Gray said she rushed to call home.
Linda Gray's 1986 megaphone, signed by the cast and crew of Dallas, is estimated to sell for $600–$800. (Julien's Auctions)

"I remember telling my kids, 'Somebody's going to call you, and they're going to ask you who shot J.R. You cannot answer.' My heart was racing because it all could have been ruined. But nobody called, thank God."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Linda Gray still loves reminiscing about her years as Sue Ellen Ewing. Now, she's passing along some of those memories through Julien's Auctions' "Ladies of the '80s," where fans can discover memorabilia from "Dallas" and celebrate one of television's most decadent decades. (Paul Archuleta/Getty Images)
Decades after "Dallas" first captivated audiences, Gray said the memories were meant to be shared.
